G1-277.h1: Where on the Number Line? 0 to 50, Labeled Every Ten
G1-277.title: Number Line to 50 Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-277.metaDescription: Number line to 50 worksheet: four lines labeled every ten with a tick at every whole number and three arrows each to name. Free printable 1st grade PDF.
G1-277.p1: A label every ten and a tick for every single number in between: that is the shape of all four lines on this 1st grade number-lines page. Each line runs from 0 to 50 and prints only 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. Three orange arrows point down at ticks that carry no number of their own, and above each arrow floats an empty dashed box. The child finds the nearest printed ten, counts on along the ticks, and writes the number the arrow lands on. Twelve answers in all, and on the last line two arrows stand close enough together to catch a child who is not really counting.
G1-277.p2: Fifty ticks on a line is a lot of small marks, and that density is what this version adds. Because the labels are ten apart, a careless route can mean nine counts, so the child who starts from zero every time runs out of patience long before the page does. The efficient reader looks at the nearest ten and then decides which way to travel: thirty-eight is two back from forty, not eight on from thirty. Choosing the shorter direction is the whole skill, and with twelve arrows there is enough repetition for it to become a habit rather than a lucky exception.
G1-277.p3: Print the PDF free and ask for the label counted from to be written in pencil beside the first box on each line, so the route is visible on the page. If the runs of single ticks cause miscounts, the counting in fives version keeps the same 0 to 50 range but prints a tick every five, which cuts the marks from fifty to ten. The 0 to 30 page is the gentler step before this one. Number of the day up to 99 puts these same two-digit numbers into tens and ones.

G1-278.h1: Number Line to 50: Every Tick Is Worth Five
G1-278.title: Number Line to 50 Counting in Fives for 1st Grade | Free PDF
G1-278.metaDescription: Counting in fives on a number line to 50: three lines with a tick every five, only 0, 25 and 50 printed, and two arrows each to name. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-278.p1: The ticks on this 1st grade number-lines page are not ones. Each step along the line is worth five, so the whole run from 0 to 50 needs only ten marks, and just three numbers are printed underneath: 0, 25 and 50. Three lines fill the page and two orange arrows point down at unnamed ticks on each of them, with an empty dashed box waiting above every arrow. Six answers altogether. To name an arrow the child counts on in fives from whichever printed number is nearest, saying thirty, thirty-five, forty rather than stepping one at a time.
G1-278.p2: Changing what a tick is worth is a bigger idea than lengthening the line. Until now every mark has meant one, and a child who keeps that assumption reads the third tick as three instead of fifteen. The page makes the assumption visible: every answer is a multiple of five, so a one-at-a-time count produces a number that does not fit the printed landmarks and the mistake shows itself. The 25 in the middle is deliberately not a ten, which stops the child leaning on decade counting and leaves the five-step chant to do the work.
G1-278.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child touch each tick while saying the fives out loud; the chant is what carries the count, and hearing it tells you whether it is secure. This is the shorter of the two counting in fives pages. The to 100 version keeps five-sized ticks but doubles the range and prints a label every ten, so the landmarks come round more often. The counting in tens page makes each tick worth ten instead, and the number walls page is where fives like these get added together.

G1-279.h1: Number Line to 100: Each Tick Counts Five
G1-279.title: Number Line to 100 Counting in Fives, 1st Grade | Free PDF
G1-279.metaDescription: Number line to 100 worksheet: four lines labeled every ten with a tick every five, and two arrows a line landing on the halfway ticks. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-279.p1: A hundred fits comfortably on one line here because each tick is worth five. Four lines cross this 1st grade number-lines page, every one labeled 0, 10, 20 and on to 100, with a single unnamed tick sitting halfway between each pair of tens. Two orange arrows point down at those halfway marks on each line, an empty dashed box above each, which gives eight answers. Every arrow therefore lands on a number ending in five, and the child has only to read the ten before it and take one step: sixty, then sixty-five.
G1-279.p2: The reasoning here is different from the pages where every tick is one. There is never more than a single step between a label and an arrow, so nothing can be lost in a long count; what is practiced instead is the pairing of tens and fives that runs all the way through place value. A child who can see that the mark between 40 and 50 must be 45, and who can say the fives in order across the whole hundred, is ready for skip counting on a hundred chart and for the halfway estimates that come later.
G1-279.p3: Print the PDF free and cover the labels on the fourth line with a strip of paper once the first three are done, to see whether the fives hold without support. The 0 to 50 counting in fives page is the same idea over half the range but with only three landmarks, which makes it harder rather than easier. The counting in tens page takes each tick up to ten, and the to 120 page carries the line past the hundred. Number of the day up to 99 works the same numbers in a different layout.

G1-280.h1: Number Line to 100: Every Tick Is a Ten
G1-280.title: Number Line to 100 Counting in Tens, 1st Grade | Free PDF
G1-280.metaDescription: Counting in tens to 100 on a number line: three lines with a tick every ten, only 0, 50 and 100 printed, and two arrows a line. Free printable 1st grade PDF.
G1-280.p1: Eleven ticks span the whole hundred on each of the three lines that make up this 1st grade number-lines page, one for every ten, and only 0, 50 and 100 are printed beneath them. Two orange arrows point down at unnamed ticks on every line, each with an empty dashed box above it, so there are six numbers to write. All six are multiples of ten, and the child reaches them by counting on in tens from the nearest of the three printed landmarks, or by counting back when the arrow sits past the middle.
G1-280.p2: This is the page where the decade sequence gets tested away from a hundred chart. Reciting ten, twenty, thirty is easy in a line; placing seventy on a real scale, and knowing it is two steps past fifty rather than three, is the part that needs practice. Because half the line lies beyond the 50 label, the child has to work in both directions, and counting back from 100 is usually the moment a teacher can see whether the decades are genuinely known or only chanted forwards. Six answers keeps it short enough for a starter.
G1-280.p3: Print the PDF free and have the child mark the middle of each line with a light pencil dot before answering, since 50 is the landmark that makes both halves manageable. The counting in fives version puts a tick every five over the same hundred and prints a label every ten, so there is more support and more to read. The to 120 page keeps ten-sized ticks but runs the line past 100, which is the natural next step. Number of the day ten more, ten less practices the same jumps without a line.

G1-281.h1: Where on the Number Line? 0 to 120, Past the Hundred
G1-281.title: Number Line to 120 Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-281.metaDescription: Number line to 120 worksheet: three lines that carry on past 100, with a tick every ten, labels at 0, 50 and 100, and two arrows each. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-281.p1: The line does not stop at the hundred. Each of the three lines on this 1st grade number-lines page runs to 120, with a tick for every ten and only 0, 50 and 100 printed, which leaves two ticks standing to the right of the last label with nothing written under them. Two orange arrows point down at unnamed ticks on each line, an empty dashed box above every one, six answers in total. Some arrows sit in the familiar part of the line and some sit out past 100, where the counting simply has to keep going.
G1-281.p2: One hundred and ten is the number that catches children out. Having spent a year treating 100 as the end of everything, they meet a tick beyond it and either stop or start again at zero. Seeing the scale carry on, with the ticks the same size and the tens still ten apart, is the argument this page makes, and it is what the first grade counting standard is really about: the sequence does not reset at a hundred. Two of the six arrows sit past the last label, enough to make the point without turning the page into a hundred-plus drill.
G1-281.p3: Print the PDF free and read the answers aloud in order once the boxes are filled, so that a hundred and ten follows a hundred by ear as well as on paper. The counting in tens page uses the same ten-sized ticks but stops at 100, and is the version to use first if the hundred itself is still new. The counting in fives pages give more landmarks over a shorter range. Number of the day up to 99 and the number walls page keep these larger numbers in play away from a scale.

G1-282.h1: Unscramble the Sentence: The Capital and End Mark Are Left In
G1-282.title: Unscramble the Sentence with Clues, 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-282.metaDescription: Sentence scramble with clues: three rows of fruit word tiles that keep their capital letter and end mark, so only the order is missing. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-282.p1: Three rows, three fruits, three sentences in pieces. A pomegranate, a blueberry and a banana sit at the left of their own cream row on this 1st grade sentence-building page, and beside each one a line of white word tiles waits out of order: this, pomegranate?, Is, your. Two tiles in every row are marked. One carries a capital letter and one carries the period or question mark, so the beginning and the end of the sentence are given away before the child starts. Underneath each row is a three-line handwriting rule for writing the sentence out.
G1-282.p2: Leaving the clues in narrows the puzzle to the middle. The child can place the capitalized tile first and the punctuated tile last without reading anything, then spend all the effort on the words in between, which is where the grammar lives. It also teaches what those two marks are for: a tile reading pomegranate? announces that the sentence will ask rather than tell, and a child who notices reads the row in a questioning voice and finds the order faster. Trying orders aloud is the method, and it is audible from across the room.
G1-282.p3: Print the PDF free and have the child number the tiles lightly in pencil before writing anything on the lines. If a row will not come, cutting the tiles out and moving them physically usually settles it in seconds. The no clues version prints sentences of the same kind with every tile in lowercase and the end mark removed, so both ends of the sentence have to be decided as well as the middle. Fix the sentence is the page along from this one, where the words are already in order and only the mechanics are missing.

G1-283.h1: Unscramble the Sentence: No Capital, No End Mark
G1-283.title: Unscramble the Sentence, No Clues, 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-283.metaDescription: Sentence scramble with no clues: four rows of animal word tiles printed all in lowercase with no end mark, so the child decides both ends. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-283.p1: Every tile on this 1st grade sentence-building page is lowercase, and not one of them carries a period. Four rows run down the sheet, each with a small picture of one of the animals at the left, a camel, a woodpecker, a penguin and a giraffe, and a set of white word tiles beside it: feeds, emma, camel, the. Even the name is printed in lowercase, so nothing on the row says where the sentence begins. The child works out the one order that makes sense, writes it on the three-line rule underneath, and adds the capital and the end mark the tiles never gave.
G1-283.p2: Taking the clues away turns a sorting task into a reading task. With no capitalized tile to anchor the first word, the child has to hear the sentence to know that Emma feeds the camel works while the camel feeds Emma, grammatical as it is, is not what the picture shows. The lowercase name is the sharpest part of the design, because a child who writes emma on the line has ordered the words correctly and still missed the rule that names take a capital wherever they stand. One row asks a question, so the end mark is a decision too.
G1-283.p3: Print the PDF free and ask for the sentence to be read aloud before the pencil moves, then read back afterwards with the capital and the mark in place. Children who order the tiles confidently but keep losing the capital are better served by the fix the sentence page, where the order is already right. The with clues version is the step back if the ordering itself is shaky. Write about the picture is where sentences like these stop being puzzles and become the child's own.

G2-281.h1: Fix the Sentence: Add the Capital Letter and the End Mark
G2-281.title: Capital Letter and End Mark Worksheet, 2nd Grade | Free PDF
G2-281.metaDescription: Fix the sentence worksheet: three animal sentences printed in lowercase with no end mark, and a two-item checklist to rewrite them by. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-281.p1: Two things are missing from every sentence on this 2nd grade capitals-punctuation page, and a dashed checklist at the top names both: Capital letter, End mark. Below it sit three cream lanes, each with a small picture of one of the animals beside a white box holding one broken sentence, printed exactly as a child would type it in a hurry: the seagulls are so big. Under each box is a three-line handwriting rule where the whole sentence is written out again, this time starting with a capital and stopping with the right mark.
G2-281.p2: None of these three sentences contains a name, which is what separates this version from its siblings. With no proper nouns to hunt for, the child has only the two ends of the sentence to think about, and the checklist can be read as a two-step routine rather than a list to remember. It is not quite as simple as adding a period every time: one of the three sentences asks a question, so the end mark still has to be chosen rather than reached for. Copying the corrected sentence in full, instead of circling the errors, is what moves the habit into the child's own writing.
G2-281.p3: Print the PDF free and have the child tick the two checklist items after each lane, then read the finished sentence back with the question mark heard rather than seen. Three lanes make this a five-minute starter or a settler after break. The choose the end mark version raises the demand to five sentences, adds names and the word I, and mixes statements with questions so the mark has to be decided every time. The unscramble the sentence pages come before this one, where the words themselves are still out of order.

G2-282.h1: Fix the Sentence: Choose Between a Period and a Question Mark
G2-282.title: Choose the End Mark Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-282.metaDescription: End mark worksheet: five lowercase sentences about fruits, some asking and some telling, to rewrite with capitals, names fixed and the right mark. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-282.p1: Can you find the pear. Where is the papaya. Read like that, two of the five sentences on this 2nd grade capitals-punctuation page are plainly wrong, and putting them right means choosing a mark rather than adding one. Five cream lanes each hold a picture of one of the fruits and a white box with a lowercase sentence inside; the checklist across the top carries three items, Capital letter, Names and End mark. One sentence hides lily, another emma, and one contains a lonely lowercase i. A three-line handwriting rule under each box takes the corrected version.
G2-282.p2: A period is what a child adds when they are not listening. This page makes that impossible by mixing three questions in among the statements, so every sentence has to be read for what it does before the mark is written. The names raise a second question the child cannot answer by position: a capital at the start is a rule about place, but the capital on lily is a rule about the word itself, and the pronoun i is the one almost every second grader still misses. Five lanes is enough to see whether all three checks are running together or only one at a time.
G2-282.p3: Print the PDF free and ask the child to read each sentence aloud with the voice going up or staying flat; the ear decides the mark faster than any rule about question words. Mark the names in a second color on the first pass if they keep escaping. The capital and end mark version is the lighter one, with three sentences, no names and a two-item checklist. Write about the picture is where these mechanics have to survive in a piece of the child's own writing.

G2-285.h1: Word Classes: Sort Nine Words, with a Picture on Every Noun
G2-285.title: Word Classes Sort for 2nd Grade, Nine Words | Free Printable PDF
G2-285.metaDescription: Word classes worksheet: nine chips, three of them animal nouns carrying a picture, to sort into labeled noun, verb and adjective bins. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-285.p1: Three of the nine word chips on this 2nd grade word-classes page carry a small picture, and all three are animals: dolphin, seagull, giraffe. The other six are plain words in the same rounded white chips, slow, swim, sit, run, purple and red, sitting in two loose rows across the top. Underneath stand three tall bins with an icon on each lid, a framed picture for nouns, a running figure for verbs and overlapping color blobs for adjectives, with the label printed below. The child reads a chip, decides which of the three it is, and writes it on a dashed line inside the right bin.
G2-285.p2: Nine chips is three for each bin, and knowing that is a legitimate strategy: a child who has placed three verbs can stop looking for a fourth. The pictures do the same work more quietly. A picture can only be pinned to a naming word, so the illustrated chips are effectively pre-sorted and the real thinking is left for the six plain ones, where the choice is between doing and describing. Colors are the easiest adjectives to recognize, which is why two of the three are here, and slow is the chip that shows whether the child is thinking about the job of a word or just its familiarity.
G2-285.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child say each word inside a short spoken sentence before writing it down, since the sentence usually settles the argument. This is the entry point of the three sorting pages. The twelve word version removes every picture and adds a fourth word to each bin; the fifteen word version stretches it further with five in each column and no support at all. The unscramble the sentence page puts words of all three kinds back into an order, which is the other half of the same idea.

G2-286.h1: Word Classes: Sort Twelve Words with No Pictures to Help
G2-286.title: Nouns Verbs Adjectives Sort, No Pictures | Free Printable PDF
G2-286.metaDescription: Word classes worksheet with no pictures: twelve plain chips, four fruit nouns among them, to read and sort into noun, verb and adjective bins. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-286.p1: Nothing on this 2nd grade word-classes page can be sorted by looking. Twelve chips lie across the top in two rows and every one is plain text: dance, coconut, watermelon, round, run, throw, sweet, soft, persimmon, laugh, red, apple. Four of them name fruits, four say what somebody does, and four describe. The three bins below are the familiar ones, an icon on each lid and nouns, verbs and adjectives printed underneath, with five dashed lines inside each. Reading is now the only route in, so the child has to work out what persimmon is without a picture confirming it.
G2-286.p2: Taking the pictures away changes who the page is for. With them, a child can sort the illustrated chips before reading a single word; without them, every chip has to be read, understood and tested. That matters most for a word like persimmon, which many second graders will not have met, and which they can still place correctly by noticing that it behaves like coconut and apple in the list. Round, sweet and soft are all sensory adjectives that pair naturally with the fruit nouns, and a child who wants to write sweet in the noun bin because it makes them think of a snack is showing exactly the confusion between a thing and a quality that the sort exists to catch.
G2-286.p3: Print the PDF free and ask for a whispered sentence before each chip is written down: I can eat a persimmon, the persimmon is sweet. The nine word version puts a picture on every noun and is the place to start if reading is still effortful. The fifteen word version keeps the plain chips and adds a fifth word to every bin. Fix the sentence and write about the picture are where these words get used rather than classified.

G2-287.h1: Word Classes: Sort Fifteen Words into Three Bins
G2-287.title: Word Classes: Sort Fifteen Words, 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-287.metaDescription: Word classes worksheet: fifteen plain chips including five vehicles, sorted five to a bin into nouns, verbs and adjectives with no pictures. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-287.p1: Fifteen chips is the fullest this sort gets. They run across the top of the 2nd grade word-classes page in two rows, all plain text, no pictures anywhere: loud, swim, gentle, small, car, run, crane, bulldozer, hot, tiny, climb, laugh, gather, airplane, motorcycle. Five of them are vehicles, five are things a person does and five describe how something is. The three bins underneath each carry six dashed lines, more than the sort needs, and the same lid icons and printed labels as the rest of the family. Every chip has to be read and placed.
G2-287.p2: Length is not the only thing that changes at fifteen. The vehicle nouns are longer and less common than the ones on the earlier pages, so bulldozer and motorcycle test reading as much as grammar, and crane is a word that names a machine here but doubles as a verb elsewhere in English, which is worth a conversation if a child hesitates over it. Gather is the least obvious verb in the set, and tiny and gentle push the adjective bin beyond color and size into quality. With five words per bin, an incomplete column is an immediate signal that something has been filed in the wrong place.
G2-287.p3: Print the PDF free and let children cross each chip off the list as they write it, since fifteen is enough for one to be missed entirely. Check the columns before the answers: five, five and five is the shape of a finished page. The twelve word version is the same task one word lighter in each bin, and the nine word version brings the pictures back for children who need the nouns confirmed. Write about the picture is where a full page of nouns, verbs and adjectives turns into sentences.

G2-289.h1: Shopping Math: Two Money Stories and a Four-Item Shelf
G2-289.title: Money Word Problems for 2nd Grade, Two Stories | Free Printable PDF
G2-289.metaDescription: Money word problems worksheet: a four-animal shelf with cent price tags and just two story cards, one total and one enough-or-not. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-289.p1: The shelf is short and so is the page. Four animals stand along the teal plank at the top of this 2nd grade money worksheet with a paper price tag hanging under each, a moose at 20¢, a hippo at 15¢, a raccoon at 10¢ and a tiger at 25¢. Only two story cards follow. In the first, Emma puts two of the animals in her basket and the question is the total; in the second, Leo has 40¢ and the child circles yes or no to whether that buys two named animals, then writes what they come to. The animals appear inside the stories as pictures, not words, so the shelf has to be read.
G2-289.p2: Two cards is a deliberate size. A money page with six problems becomes an endurance test, and the child who understands the first two learns nothing from the next four; the child who does not understand them is stuck six times over. Cutting the page to one addition and one comparison leaves room to talk. Putting the pictures rather than the names in the story text is the quiet demand here: before any arithmetic happens, the child has to look up two tags, which is the shop-reading skill the whole family is built on.
G2-289.p3: Print the PDF free and use it as a first meeting with the shelf, working the two cards together before setting a longer version alone. The dot grid inside each card is there for jottings, and the small ¢ printed beside the answer box is a reminder that the unit belongs in the answer. Add up the basket goes on to three straight totals, and the four questions page puts one of each type on a single sheet once all four are familiar. Counting coins is the page to visit first if coin values are still uncertain.

G2-290.h1: Shopping Math: Four Cards, Four Different Questions
G2-290.title: Shopping Math: Four Money Questions, 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-290.metaDescription: Money worksheet with four cards: find a three-item total, work out change from two coins, decide if there is enough, and compare two prices. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-290.p1: No two cards ask the same thing here. The shelf on this 2nd grade money worksheet holds five vehicles with tags reading 40¢, 15¢, 45¢, 30¢ and 10¢, and the four cards below run through the whole repertoire: Mia buys three of them and pays how much, Max buys one and pays with two coins drawn as circles marked 25 so the change has to be found, Lily has 55¢ and the child circles yes or no then writes the total, and the last card asks how much more one vehicle costs than another. Each card has a dot grid to work on and a dashed answer box with ¢ beside it.
G2-290.p2: Mixing the four types is a harder job than any one of them, because the child can no longer run the same procedure down the page. Deciding whether a story wants adding, taking away or comparing is the part of word problems that transfers, and it only gets practiced when the question changes from card to card. The order is deliberate too: the total comes first as the most familiar, and the how much more card comes last, since difference is the type most often answered by adding out of habit.
G2-290.p3: Print the PDF free and ask the child to say what each card is asking before any numbers are written, in their own words. If one type collapses, the single-type pages are the place to repair it: add up the basket for totals, how much change for coins and change, is there enough money for the yes-or-no compare, and how much more for differences. Come back to this page afterwards, since telling the four apart is what it is for. The multiplication and division word problems page carries the same reading habit into third grade.

G2-291.h1: Add Up the Basket: Every Card Asks for the Total
G2-291.title: Adding Prices Worksheet: Add Up the Basket | Free Printable PDF
G2-291.metaDescription: Adding money worksheet: a five-toy shelf with cent tags and three cards that all ask for a total of two prices, with a dot grid to work on. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-291.p1: Every card on this 2nd grade money worksheet asks the same question. Five toys hang their price tags from the shelf at the top, a truck at 15¢, a pack of cards at 45¢, a balloon at 20¢, a chess piece at 25¢ and a dinosaur at 40¢, and the three story cards underneath each name two of them and want the total. Emma wants two things, Ben puts two in the basket, Anna buys two: the wording changes, the arithmetic does not. Each card gives a dot grid to work on and a dashed box with ¢ for the answer.
G2-291.p2: Repeating the question is the point of this version. When the type is fixed, the child stops spending attention on what is being asked and puts it into how to add two two-digit numbers, and the three cards become three attempts at the same method rather than three separate puzzles. All the prices are multiples of five, so the totals stay friendly and can be reached by counting on in fives, in tens, or by splitting the tens from the ones. Watching which of those three routes a child takes is more informative than the answer.
G2-291.p3: Print the PDF free and use it as the settling page after a mixed sheet has shown that totals are shaky. Ask for the two prices to be copied onto the dot grid before adding, so the working shows where a mistake happened. The buying three things version keeps the same question but puts three prices in every basket, which forces a strategy rather than a fact. The two stories page is shorter, and the four questions page brings change and comparison back in once adding is reliable.

G2-292.h1: Shopping Math: Three Prices in Every Basket
G2-292.title: Adding Three Prices Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-292.metaDescription: Money worksheet for adding three prices: a fruit shelf with cent tags and three baskets that each hold three items to total. Free printable 2nd grade PDF.
G2-292.p1: Three prices go into every answer on this 2nd grade money worksheet. The shelf carries five fruits and their tags, a strawberry at 15¢, a pineapple at 20¢, a kiwi at 10¢, a mango at 25¢ and a banana at 45¢, and each of the three cards below shows a child taking three of them, drawn as pictures inside the sentence. Leo buys three, Emma takes three, Max buys three. The dot grid on each card is wide enough for the running total, and the answer goes in the dashed box with ¢ printed at its side.
G2-292.p2: A third addend changes the mathematics, not just the length of the sum. Two prices can be held in the head; three cannot, so the child has to write something down, and that is where strategy appears. Some will add left to right and carry a running total, some will look for a pair that makes fifty, some will collect the tens first and then the fives. All three work, and all three are worth naming aloud when they happen. The prices are chosen so that a friendly pair usually exists, which rewards the child who looks at all three numbers before starting.
G2-292.p3: Print the PDF free and ask for the three prices to be listed under one another on the dot grid before anything is added, which turns the story into a column the child can check. If the totals go wrong at the third number rather than the second, the add up the basket page steps back to two items with the same shelf format. The four questions page mixes these totals with change and comparison. Number walls practices the same adding in a shape with no shopping attached.

G2-293.h1: Shopping Math: Count the Coins, Then Work Out the Change
G2-293.title: Making Change Worksheet for 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-293.metaDescription: Making change worksheet: two animal shop stories where the coins paid are drawn on the card as circles marked 25, and the change has to be found. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-293.p1: The money paid is drawn on the card. Both stories on this 2nd grade money worksheet show two teal circles marked 25 sitting inside the sentence, so the child counts the coins to fifty before anything else happens. The shelf above holds five animals with tags reading 40¢, 20¢, 35¢, 30¢ and 45¢. Mia pays for one animal with those two coins and the card asks how much money she gets back; Leo does the same with another and the card asks for his change. Each has a dot grid and a dashed answer box marked ¢.
G2-293.p2: Change is the money question children find hardest, because the story runs forwards and the arithmetic runs backwards. Two things have to be sorted out in order: what was handed over, which the drawn coins make countable rather than assumed, and what it cost, which the shelf supplies. Only then does the subtraction appear. Most second graders solve it by counting up from the price to the fifty rather than taking one number from the other, and that method is worth encouraging on the dot grid, because it is the method a shopkeeper uses and it survives into larger amounts.
G2-293.p3: Print the PDF free and put two real quarters on the desk beside the page; the drawn coins are clear but handling them makes the fifty concrete. Ask for the price and the amount paid to be written down before the change is worked out, so a wrong answer can be traced to the right step. Is there enough money is the companion comparison page, and add up the basket is where totals are practiced alone. Counting coins is the page to use first if a child cannot yet read two quarters as fifty cents.

G2-294.h1: Is There Enough Money? Circle Yes or No, Then Write the Total
G2-294.title: Is There Enough Money? 2nd Grade Worksheet | Free Printable PDF
G2-294.metaDescription: Money comparison worksheet: two vehicle shop stories where the child adds two prices, circles yes or no, and writes the total in cents. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-294.p1: Yes and no sit in two outlined ovals beside the working box on both cards of this 2nd grade money worksheet, and neither can be circled honestly until the adding is done. Five vehicles hold up the shelf at the top with tags at 15¢, 20¢, 40¢, 35¢ and 30¢. Anna has 45¢ and wants two of them; Emma has 40¢ and wants two others. Each card gives the amount in the pocket, shows the two vehicles as pictures, and asks for the circle and then the total in a dashed box marked ¢.
G2-294.p2: This is the one money question that ends in a judgment rather than a number, and it is the reason the page also asks for the total. A child can circle yes or no by feel, and about half the time be right; writing the total underneath forces the comparison to be made rather than guessed, and it shows the teacher whether a correct circle came from correct arithmetic. Comparing a sum against an amount in hand is also the most common piece of real shopping arithmetic there is, which is why it earns a page of its own rather than one card in a mixed set.
G2-294.p3: Print the PDF free and check the totals before the circles when marking, since a right circle over a wrong total is the answer to watch for. Asking how much more would be needed, or how much would be left, extends either card into a spoken problem without any more paper. How much change is the companion page where money is handed over and returned, and add up the basket is where the totals themselves are practiced. The four questions page is where this type sits beside the other three.

G2-295.h1: Shopping Math: How Much More Does One Toy Cost Than Another?
G2-295.title: How Much More Does It Cost? Money Worksheet | Free Printable PDF
G2-295.metaDescription: Comparing prices worksheet: three cards that each pair two toys from the shelf and ask for the difference between their prices in cents. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-295.p1: Nothing is bought on this 2nd grade money worksheet. Five toys hang from the shelf with their tags, a boat at 40¢, a set of dominoes at 30¢, a robot at 10¢, a slide at 35¢ and a rocket at 20¢, and all three cards below pair two of them and ask for the gap between the prices. Two cards put it as a question, how much more does one cost than the other, and one puts it as a statement followed by a question, the slide costs more than the rocket, how much more? The answer goes in a dashed box marked ¢ after working on the dot grid.
G2-295.p2: Difference is the money question children answer by adding, and the wording is why. How much more sounds like more, and more sounds like plus, so the child who is matching key words to operations rather than picturing the situation gets it exactly backwards. Two prices side by side on a shelf make the gap visible, which is the correction: the child can see that one tag is bigger and that the question is about the space between them. The reversed phrasing on the third card is a deliberate check that the reading is real and not a template.
G2-295.p3: Print the PDF free and have the two prices written one under the other before anything is worked out, or counted up from the smaller tag to the larger on the dot grid, which is the safer method for most second graders. Comparing three-digit numbers gives the same comparison without money. Is there enough money is the other comparison page, ending in a yes or no instead of a gap, and the four questions page puts differences back among totals and change.

G2-296.h1: Read the Calendar: A First Look at the Month
G2-296.title: Reading a Calendar Worksheet, Four Questions | Free Printable PDF
G2-296.metaDescription: Calendar worksheet for a first look: one full month with two picture stickers and four short questions about days, dates and month length. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-296.p1: One month, printed properly. This 2nd grade calendar worksheet shows August 2026 as a full grid with Sun to Sat across a teal header, every date in its own cell, and two small stickers dropped onto the month, a soccer ball on one Friday and a little figure on another. Four questions follow in cream boxes laid out two by two, each with a dashed space for the answer: what day of the week the 6th falls on, how many Thursdays the month contains, on which date the ball sticker sits, and how many days the month has altogether.
G2-296.p2: Four questions is enough to cover the three ways a calendar gets read and no more. One asks the child to go from a date to a weekday, which means finding a cell and looking up to the header. One asks them to count down a column, which is the reading direction children miss most often, since a calendar looks like rows. One sends them hunting for a picture, and the last is answered by finding the largest number on the grid rather than by counting anything. Keeping the set short means a child can finish it and be talked through all four while the page is still fresh.
G2-296.p3: Print the PDF free and lay it beside the calendar on the classroom wall, asking the same four questions of the real month afterwards. If a child answers the Thursday question by counting every cell, show them the column once and ask again. The busy month version raises this to five questions on a six-row month with three stickers and adds a how many days between question; the days of the week version keeps four questions but makes every one of them about weekdays. The telling time pages are the other clock-and-calendar practice in the catalog.

G2-297.h1: Read the Calendar: A Busy Month with Five Questions
G2-297.title: Calendar Worksheet for 2nd Grade: A Busy Month | Free Printable PDF
G2-297.metaDescription: Calendar worksheet: a six-row month carrying three stickers, with five questions including one week later and how many days between two events. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-297.p1: August 2025 begins on a Friday, which is why it needs six rows and ends with the 31st sitting alone on the bottom line. That crowded shape is the point of this 2nd grade calendar worksheet. Three stickers are scattered across the month, a stack of blocks, a pair of playing cards and a die, and five questions follow beneath the grid: the weekday of the 29th, how many Mondays the month holds, the date the blocks sit on, the date one week after the 10th, and how many days lie between the blocks and the die.
G2-297.p2: Two of these five questions cannot be answered by reading a single cell. One week after the 10th is the classic calendar insight, because the answer is the cell directly below rather than seven cells counted forward, and the child who has understood the grid finds it instantly while the child who has not counts along the row and wraps around. The days between question is harder still: it spans three weeks and two stickers, and it can be solved by counting cells, by counting whole weeks and adding the remainder, or by subtracting the dates. All three are correct and each says something different about where the child is.
G2-297.p3: Print the PDF free and ask for the two hard questions to be answered with a finger on the grid before the pencil, so the route is visible. Marking the two sticker dates in pencil first makes the between question far less slippery. The first look version is the same page shape with four questions, two stickers and a shorter month, and is the one to hand out if the six-row grid causes trouble by itself. The days of the week version drills weekday reading alone.

G2-298.h1: Read the Calendar: Every Question Is About the Days
G2-298.title: Days of the Week Calendar Worksheet, 2nd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G2-298.metaDescription: Calendar worksheet on days of the week: read down the columns to answer what day the 10th is, how many Wednesdays, and the first and last day. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-298.p1: Every one of the four questions on this 2nd grade calendar worksheet is answered with the name of a day. May 2027 is printed as a full grid, Sun to Sat, with two stickers sitting on the month as decoration rather than as anything to look up. The questions ask what day of the week the 10th falls on, how many Wednesdays there are, what day the month starts on and what day it ends on. Each has a dashed box underneath, and each is answered by moving between a cell and the weekday header above it.
G2-298.p2: Narrowing every question to the days turns the page into a column-reading exercise. To count the Wednesdays a child has to travel straight down one column, and to name the first and last day of the month they have to notice that a month rarely starts on a Sunday or ends on a Saturday, which is why the grid has blank cells at both ends. Children who can recite the seven days in order often cannot yet do any of this, because reciting is a chain and reading a calendar is a table. The first and last day questions also plant the idea that the same date is a different weekday next month.
G2-298.p3: Print the PDF free and have the child trace one column top to bottom with a finger before writing the count, then check by looking at the header they landed under. Spelling the day names is part of the work here, so leave the wall calendar visible rather than correcting from memory. The first look version mixes weekday questions with dates and month length; the busy month version adds date arithmetic on a six-row grid. Alphabetical order is the other page that has children writing the day and month names carefully.

G2-299.h1: Write About the Picture: Sentence Starters and a Word Bank
G2-299.title: Write About the Picture: Sentence Starters | Free Printable PDF
G2-299.metaDescription: Picture writing worksheet with sentence starters: an animal scene, a four-word picture bank, and rows beginning I can see, It is and I like the. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-299.p1: Five animals stand in a framed scene at the top of this 2nd grade picture-writing page, two raccoons, a fox, a panda and an antelope, arranged with space around them so each one can be looked at on its own. Under the frame a dashed word bank holds four picture chips with their names printed underneath, antelope, raccoon, fox and panda. Then come the writing rows, and the first three begin with a faint starter already on the line: I can see, It is, I like the. The rows after them are empty.
G2-299.p2: These starters ask for description, not a story. I can see opens a sentence about what is there, It is asks what something is like, and I like the invites an opinion, so the child ends up writing three different kinds of sentence about one picture rather than three versions of the same one. That is a gentler job than inventing events, and it is the right job for a writer who can form a sentence but freezes at a blank line. The word bank removes spelling from the decision, which matters when the noun is antelope. A teacher can read the three rows and see whether the child varied the sentence or only swapped the animal.
G2-299.p3: Print the PDF free and have the child point at what they are about to write about before starting each row, then read the finished rows back in order. The empty rows below the starters are for children who keep going, and for the ones who need a fourth sentence modeled orally. The your own words version takes the starters away entirely and gives a six-word bank, which is the next step once the sentences arrive without prompting. Fix the sentence is where the capitals and end marks used here are practiced on their own.

G2-300.h1: Write About the Picture in Your Own Words: No Starters
G2-300.title: Picture Writing Prompt, No Sentence Starters | Free Printable PDF
G2-300.metaDescription: Picture writing worksheet with no starters: a fruit scene, a six-word picture bank, and a page of empty handwriting rows for the child to fill. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-300.p1: Not a single word is printed on the writing lines of this 2nd grade picture-writing page. A scene of fruits fills the frame at the top, a large strawberry in front with an apple, a plum, a nectarine and two mangoes around it, and beneath it a dashed word bank offers six picture chips with names, strawberry, mango, nectarine, plum, cranberry and peach. Everything below that is empty rule, row after row of it, waiting for whatever the child decides to write about the picture.
G2-300.p2: Removing the starters removes the safety and hands over the decision. A child who writes I can see a strawberry has written a caption; a child who writes about a picnic, or about which fruit they would take, has written something of their own, and only a blank line lets that happen. The six-chip bank is doing the same work it always does, keeping spelling out of the way, and it is a chip longer than the version with starters, so there is more vocabulary and more room to roam. Note that the bank names a cranberry and a peach the scene does not obviously show, so the child chooses their words rather than labeling what is in front of them.
G2-300.p3: Print the PDF free and give a minute of talking before the pencil, since children who have said their first sentence aloud almost always write it. Do not expect the whole rule to be filled; three good sentences on a page this open is a strong result. The what you see version prints I can see, It is and I like the on the first three rows and is the page to fall back on if the blank sheet stalls. Fix the sentence and the word classes sort are where the mechanics and the vocabulary get their own practice.

G2-302.h1: Grid Coordinates on a 6x6 Grid: Color the Squares
G2-302.title: Grid Coordinates Worksheet: 6x6 Grid | Free Printable PDF
G2-302.metaDescription: Coordinate grid worksheet on a 6x6 grid: letters A to F, numbers 1 to 6, a worked B2 example, and about twenty codes to color in. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-302.p1: The grid on this 2nd grade grid-coordinates page is six squares by six, lettered A to F along the top and numbered 1 to 6 down the side, and it starts completely empty. Beside it sits a small worked example, a three-by-three grid with one square shaded and B2 printed underneath, so the child sees what a code means before reading any. The key below the grid is short: a yellow swatch followed by twenty code chips, B1, D5, E4 and the rest, and an orange swatch followed by a single chip, E2. Find each square, color it, and a picture appears.
G2-302.p2: Thirty-six squares is a grid a second grader can hold in view, and that is what makes this the version to start on. The letters run only as far as F, so the across-then-down habit gets built on a short alphabet, and a misread code shows up quickly because there is nowhere for a wrong square to hide. The lone orange chip is worth pointing out: one square in a second color is usually the detail that makes the picture readable, an eye or a spot, and a child who colors it yellow by mistake will see the difference immediately.
G2-302.p3: Print the PDF free and have the child cross off each chip as its square is filled, since the codes are shuffled rather than ordered and skipping one is the easiest mistake to make. The classic error is reading B2 as row B, column 2, which puts squares in the wrong half of the grid and bends the picture out of shape. The 10x10 version keeps the same rules over a hundred squares with about thirty codes. Copy the grid picture is the kindergarten ancestor of this page, where squares are matched by position without any codes at all.

G2-303.h1: Grid Coordinates on a 10x10 Grid: A Hundred Squares
G2-303.title: Grid Coordinates Worksheet: 10x10 Grid | Free Printable PDF
G2-303.metaDescription: Coordinate grid worksheet on a 10x10 grid: columns A to J, rows 1 to 10, and about thirty color-coded squares to find and fill in. Free 2nd grade PDF.
G2-303.p1: A hundred empty squares wait on this 2nd grade grid-coordinates page, ten across lettered A to J and ten down numbered 1 to 10, with the same small worked example beside them showing B2 shaded on a three-by-three grid. The key underneath is longer than on the smaller version: a red swatch with about two dozen chips, F4, B5, D3 and on through the list, then a brown swatch with five more, D10, D7, C10, D9 and D8. The child locates each square by its letter and number and colors it in the group color.
G2-303.p2: Doubling the grid does more than add squares. The columns now run past the halfway point of the alphabet, so a child cannot count the letters on one hand, and a row like 7 sits far enough from both edges that the finger has to travel carefully rather than land by feel. Two colors keep the sorting manageable while the locating gets harder. The codes on this sheet stay in the left and middle columns, so the last two columns finish the page still blank, and a child who has been coloring squares out on the right has misread the letter axis rather than the number.
G2-303.p3: Print the PDF free and ask for the letter to be found first and the finger held on it while the number is counted down, which is the habit that survives into coordinates on a graph. Crossing off each chip is close to essential at thirty codes. The 6x6 version is the same task on a grid a child can take in at a glance and is where to begin. Reading a calendar uses the same across-and-down table reading in a form the child will meet on the wall every day.

G3-371.h1: Multiplication Word Problems: The Groups Are Drawn for You
G3-371.title: Multiplication Word Problems for 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-371.metaDescription: Multiplication word problems: two animal stories about equal rows and groups, each with the groups drawn in outlined boxes underneath. Free 3rd grade PDF.
G3-371.p1: Both stories on this 3rd grade word-problems page multiply, and both show their groups. Ben sets out 3 rows of swans with 2 in each row, and under the sentence three small outlined boxes hold two swans apiece; Tom makes 4 groups of zebras with 4 in each, and four boxes hold four zebras each. The animals are drawn inside the boxes so the grouping is visible rather than described. Each card then gives a dot grid to work on, a dashed box for the number, and a handwriting line underneath for the answer written as a sentence.
G3-371.p2: Drawing the groups is what makes this the first multiplication page rather than a test. A child who cannot yet reach for 3 times 2 can count the swans, and in counting them can see why the numbers in the story are a count of groups and a count inside each group, which is the whole idea the notation stands for. The two stories use different words for the same structure, rows in one and groups in the other, so the child learns that a row of a picture and a group of a story are the same thing. The answer sentence matters as much as the box: writing there are 6 swans says what the number counts.
G3-371.p3: Print the PDF free and ask for the multiplication sentence to be written on the dot grid beside the counting, so the picture and the symbols end up next to one another. Products here stay small enough for the picture to fit on the card. The sharing and the making groups pages take the same layout into division, and the two ways page puts both kinds of division on one sheet. The mixed problems page is the last of the family, where the child has to decide which operation a story wants before starting.

G3-372.h1: Division Word Problems: Share the Fruits Out Equally
G3-372.title: Division Word Problems: Sharing, 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-372.metaDescription: Sharing division word problems: fruits pictured above empty dashed boxes so the child can deal them out equally before writing the answer. Free 3rd grade PDF.
G3-372.p1: Twenty persimmons sit in two neat rows above five empty dashed boxes. That picture is the whole method of this 3rd grade word-problems page: the fruits are all there, the boxes are all there, and nothing is in them yet. Ben sorts the persimmons equally into 5 groups and the child works out how many land in each; below, Mia lines 10 papayas up over 2 empty boxes and the question is how many go in each row. A dot grid, a dashed answer box and a handwriting line for the answer sentence finish each card.
G3-372.p2: This is sharing division, the kind where the number of groups is known and the size of each group is not. Children meet it first because it matches something they have done since they were three, dealing things out one at a time until they run out, and the empty boxes invite exactly that. Dealing is slow but it is not a trick; it produces the right answer and it shows the child why the answer is a group size. The step from there is noticing that a fair deal can be predicted, that twenty into five must be four because five fours are twenty, which is where the multiplication facts come back in.
G3-372.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child tally into the boxes with pencil dots rather than drawing whole fruits, which keeps the dealing quick enough to stay useful. If the deal comes out uneven, the count of the original picture is usually where it went wrong. The making groups page is the other kind of division, where the group size is given and the number of groups has to be found, and the two ways page prints one of each so they can be compared. The multiplication word problems page is the one to secure first.

G3-373.h1: Division Word Problems: Ring the Equal Groups Yourself
G3-373.title: Division Word Problems: Making Equal Groups | Free Printable PDF
G3-373.metaDescription: Grouping division word problems: toys pictured in one loose row with no boxes, so the child rings equal groups and counts how many there are. Free 3rd grade PDF.
G3-373.p1: Nothing is boxed on this 3rd grade word-problems page. The toys in both stories, eight airplanes on the first card and eight kites on the second, are printed in a single loose row with no divisions drawn anywhere, and the instruction asks the child to ring the equal groups in the picture. Ben makes groups of 4 from the airplanes and the question is how many groups; Mia puts 2 kites in each group and the question is the same. Under each row is a dot grid, a dashed answer box and a line for the answer sentence.
G3-373.p2: This is the other division, and it is the one that gets skipped. Here the size of each group is given and the number of groups is what has to be found, which is a genuinely different action from dealing things out: the child circles four, circles four more, and counts the circles rather than the objects. Because the pencil has to make the groups, the page cannot be answered by looking, and a child who rings unequal groups has shown the misunderstanding on the paper where it can be talked about. The same eight objects split two ways across the two cards, into groups of four and groups of two, which is a quiet demonstration that the total does not change when the group size does.
G3-373.p3: Print the PDF free and insist on the rings before the answer box, in pencil so they can be redrawn. Counting the rings aloud at the end, two groups, four groups, is what connects the picture to the division sentence. The sharing page is the companion where the boxes are already drawn and the child deals into them; running the two on consecutive days makes the contrast clear. The two ways page puts one of each on a single sheet, and the mixed problems page adds multiplication back into the choice.

G3-374.h1: Division Two Ways: Sharing on One Card, Grouping on the Other
G3-374.title: Two Kinds of Division Word Problems, 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-374.metaDescription: Division word problems two ways: one card shares fruits into given boxes, the other rings equal groups in a loose row. Both are division. Free 3rd grade PDF.
G3-374.p1: The two cards on this 3rd grade word-problems page look different on purpose. On the first, twelve nectarines are pictured above two wide empty boxes, and Tom sorts them equally into 2 groups; on the second, ten cranberries lie in one unbroken row with no boxes at all, and Tom arranges them in rows of 5. Both stories are about fruits, both are division, and only the first supplies the containers. Each card carries the usual dot grid, a dashed answer box and a handwriting line for the sentence.
G3-374.p2: Putting the two shapes side by side is the point. Sharing gives the number of groups and asks for the size; grouping gives the size and asks for the number, and although both are written with a division sign, children who have only met one of them will try to run its method on the other and find no boxes to deal into. Seeing them on one sheet, in the same layout with the same kind of picture, is what makes the difference discussable: what does this story already tell me, and what is it asking for? That question, rather than any procedure, is what a word problems page is for.
G3-374.p3: Print the PDF free and ask, before any working, which card gives the boxes and which does not; the answer names the type without any vocabulary being required. If one card is much harder than the other, its single-type page is the repair: sharing for the dealt boxes, making groups for the rings. The mixed problems page adds a multiplication story to the same choice, and the multiplication word problems page is where the equal-groups picture is first built rather than broken up.

G3-375.h1: Multiply and Group: One Story Builds, One Story Breaks Up
G3-375.title: Multiply and Group: Word Problems 3rd Grade | Free Printable PDF
G3-375.metaDescription: Word problems worksheet: one animal story builds 3 rows of 5 into a total, the next breaks 12 into groups of 2. Multiplication beside division. Free 3rd grade PDF.
G3-375.p1: Three rows of five woodpeckers, drawn in three outlined boxes, and then twelve koalas in no boxes at all. Those two pictures carry the two stories on this 3rd grade word-problems page. Mia sees 3 rows with 5 woodpeckers in each and the question is how many animals there are altogether; Leo has 12 koalas and makes groups of 2, and the question is how many groups. The first card hands the child the groups and asks for the total, the second hands over the total and asks for the groups. Both give a dot grid, a dashed box and a line for the answer sentence.
G3-375.p2: This pairing is the cleanest picture of inverse operations a third grader can be given. One story starts from equal groups and ends at a total; the other starts from a total and ends at equal groups, and the pictures show it, boxes already drawn on the first card and a bare row on the second. A child who has just multiplied three fives to reach fifteen has a way of thinking about twelve broken into twos that is not counting, and the moment they use their multiplication to predict the number of groups is the moment the two operations join up.
G3-375.p3: Print the PDF free and ask for both answers to be written as multiplication and division sentences on the dot grid, one under the other, before the boxes are filled. Two cards make this a short lesson rather than a worksheet session. The multiplication word problems page has two building stories and no breaking; the two ways page has two breaking stories and no building. The mixed problems page carries three stories and asks the child to sort out which is which without the layout hinting at it.

G3-376.h1: Mixed Problems: Three Stories, and You Decide What Each Asks
G3-376.title: Mixed Multiplication and Division Word Problems | Free Printable PDF
G3-376.metaDescription: Mixed word problems: three toy stories on one page, one multiplication, one sharing division and one grouping division, in no helpful order. Free 3rd grade PDF.
G3-376.p1: Three cards fit on this 3rd grade word-problems page rather than the usual two, and each one is a different kind of problem. Leo sees 3 rows of 4 legos, drawn in three outlined boxes, and the total is wanted; Mia shares 18 skateboards equally among 6 friends, pictured above six empty dashed boxes to deal into; and 18 cars lie in one loose row with no boxes while Leo makes groups of 6. The toys change, the layout of each picture changes, and the child has to read before working. Dot grid, dashed answer box and answer line on every card.
G3-376.p2: This is the page that tests the reading rather than the arithmetic. The three story shapes are the ones the family has taught separately, equal groups to a total, a total shared into a known number of groups, and a total broken into groups of a known size, and here they arrive in one place with nothing announcing which is which. The pictures still help, but they help only after the child has understood the sentence, since the six empty boxes on the second card mean nothing until the story has explained what goes in them. The last two stories both start from 18, which stops a child guessing the operation from the size of the number.
G3-376.p3: Print the PDF free and use it as the check at the end of the unit, not the introduction. Ask for one sentence of explanation per card, in the child's own words, before the working; that sentence is where a wrong operation shows itself while it can still be fixed. If one type keeps going astray, its single-type page is the place to go back to. Multiply and group is the two-card version of this same idea, and the arrays multiplication page is where equal groups first become rows and columns.
